transcript:
Header: 2025-08-20 14:00 PDT / Duration: 68 minutes / Attendees: Alice Kim (AE, Redwood); Marco Liu (SE, Redwood); Jake Brooks (CTO, Polaris Health); Priya Singh (Eng Manager); Rohan Patel (Data Eng)

00:00 Alice Kim: hey everyone, thanks for carving the time, um this is the benchmark methodology workshop, the goal is to get a repeatable apples-to-apples process for runtime comparisons across hosted, dedicated and private runs.
00:18 Jake Brooks: yeah thanks Alice, we wanna make sure when we run perf tests with a vendor it's comparable, we spent weeks troubleshooting differences last time, so...
00:30 Marco Liu: totally, and the main culprits we see are tokenization mismatches, different sampling settings, and KV cache warm up, plus the way load is generated can mask latency p95.
00:45 Priya Singh: can you define apples-to-apples for us? like what are the must-haves?
00:52 Marco Liu: sure — short list: identical model weights (same checkpoint & math precision), same tokenizer and pre/post processing, fixed seed/deterministic generation for generation latency tests, identical context/seq length distribution, and identical batching policies when possible. Also capture cold-start and steady-state separately.
01:12 Rohan Patel: when you say "identical batching policies" do you mean we need to replicate the server batching algorithm locally? that's hard.
01:20 Marco Liu: yeah, so we recommend two comparators: 1) an isolated single-request latency test (no batching, 1 thread) and 2) a throughput test using a load-generator that simulates realistic arrival patterns — Poisson or production trace — and then measure p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec, plus record batch-size distributions. You don't have to copy server internals, but you should force the same max batch size and request arrival characteristics.
01:45 Jake Brooks: cool, what about KV cache — our workload is very chatty, lots of repeated prefixes.
01:52 Marco Liu: KV cache will dominate token generation cost for chatty sessions. Important notes: KV cache warm-up means first requests will be cold and behave like full attention compute; after k steps the cache fills and subsequent token generation is much faster. For benching — you should run a warm-up phase per session template and then measure steady-state. Also capture time-to-warm (how many tokens/requests) and measure both cold and warm p95.
02:18 Priya Singh: any heuristics for warm-up length?
02:22 Marco Liu: depends on typical session length — if most sessions are 200 tokens then warm-up may be 10-20 tokens for KV indexing depending on model. We usually recommend running 10x your 95th percentile session length in a synthetic warm-up to be safe for benchmarks.
02:40 Alice Kim: quick note on metrics — record CPU/GPU utilization, memory usage, GPU power draw, tokens/sec, latency histograms, batch size distribution, queue times, and network egress numbers for private setups.
02:56 Rohan Patel: good point on network — for on-prem we will have local NVLink but for VPC we might see egress between zones, how do we normalize that?
03:08 Marco Liu: capture network RTTs and measure end-to-end latency with and without network hop simulation. For apples-to-apples, if you're comparing hosted vs private, either run both in same region or add an artificial network delay to the private runs to match hosted path — or report both raw and network-normalized numbers.
03:30 Jake Brooks: quantization — we are very interested in INT8 to cut cost but worried about subtle accuracy regressions. Thoughts?
03:38 Marco Liu: quantization (INT8, Q4/Q5 variants) gives big perf wins but you must do token-level quality checks. We suggest: 1) run identical prompts with FP16/FP32 and quantized variants, 2) compute exact-match / BLEU-like heuristics for structured outputs or embedding cosine similarity for embedding tasks, 3) run your core prompt set and a few hard prompts that stress arithmetic or long-range context. Also tie quality thresholds to acceptance criteria in the benchmark spreadsheet.
04:08 Priya Singh: for generation randomness — temperature/top_p — you recommended fixed-seed for latency tests but for quality we should sample?
04:17 Marco Liu: exactly. For latency/throughput apples-to-apples, use deterministic sampling (seed, temperature=0 or greedy) to remove variance; for quality/regression checks run at production sampling settings and measure distributional metrics across the prompt set.
04:33 Alice Kim: any tips on prompt set construction?
04:36 Marco Liu: yes: include typical short prompts (10-30 tokens), medium (100-300), and long-context templates (500+). Include edge cases like multi-turn chats, many named entities, and prompts that force the longest attention windows. Also include real production samples if possible — Rohan, can you share anonymized prompt set?
04:55 Rohan Patel: yes, I'll export a representative sample and send — expect it by Monday.
05:00 Jake Brooks: load generation tools — what do you recommend?
05:04 Marco Liu: for steady-state and arrival patterns we like Locust for trace-driven tests, k6 for HTTP-based throughput, and wrk for simple concurrency tests. Important: avoid simplistic constant QPS; use Poisson arrivals or replay a real trace. Also run multiple trials at different concurrency levels to find knee in latency vs throughput curve.
05:30 Priya Singh: how do you measure batch distribution? metrics on the server?
05:34 Marco Liu: yes server should emit per-request batch-size and queue time to correlate latency spikes with oversized batches. We'll provide a small instrumentation patch that emits these metrics; we'll share that repo link in the notes.
05:48 Alice Kim: SECURITY quick check — Polaris asked about KMS and audit logs earlier — where do those fit into benching?
05:56 Marco Liu: security doesn't directly change perf but encryption and KMS calls can add micro-latency on key unwrap for cold starts; for on-prem with HSM it may affect cold start. So include a bench variant with KMS enabled and another with KMS bypassed (only for perf testing) and report both; obviously production must use KMS. Also capture logs size and retention if you're worried about storage costs.
06:24 Jake Brooks: good to know. Ok, what about measurement windows? steady-state length?
06:29 Marco Liu: for steady-state we recommend at least 10 minutes after warm-up per trial and run 3 trials, compare variance. For long-running throughput stress tests run 60-minute windows to catch GC/thermal throttling effects.
06:46 Rohan Patel: do you have a template spreadsheet?
06:49 Alice Kim: yes — link to benchmarking-playbook + a results spreadsheet: https://redwood.ai/bench-playbook (we'll attach real links in follow-up)
07:00 Priya Singh: excellent. One more — apples-to-apples when vendors use different model variants (e.g., pruned or optimized kernels) — how strict are we?
07:10 Marco Liu: rule of thumb: if the weights differ, call it out — report respective sizes and FLOPs. For kernel-level optimizations that's fine but document optimizations applied. If comparing quantized vs fp16, run both under same inference engine when possible.
07:28 Jake Brooks: let's capture P95 and P99 as the primary SLO metrics, and tokens/sec for throughput.
07:34 Marco Liu: agreed. Also capture distribution of session lengths because batching efficiency depends heavily on that.
07:40 Alice Kim: wrap-up and next steps — recap?
07:44 Jake Brooks: recap: SE runs apples-to-apples bench and shares spreadsheet, we provide prompt set and seq length distribution, Redwood sends SOC2 and on-prem packaging notes, and schedule sizing call.
07:56 Alice Kim: yep, that's what we have on our side. We'll also include the instrumentation patch and an example Locust script.
08:04 Marco Liu: ok I'll run the bench with the following constraints: same weights/tokenizer, deterministic seeds for latency tests, warm-up of 10x p95 seq length, report cold and warm p95/p99 and batch-size distributions, and include quantized vs fp16 runs. I'll share raw logs and a cleaned results sheet.
08:24 Rohan Patel: thanks Marco. One small point — in our environment we use a mixed sequence distribution that is heavy on short requests, will that affect batching?
08:32 Marco Liu: yes, skewed short-request workloads reduce batching benefits; that's why the batch-size distribution is critical to interpret tokens/sec. If you want batch-friendly behavior, config autoscaler and paddle windows but that's a bigger ops change.
08:48 Priya Singh: do you have any specific guidance for VPC private deployments — e.g., NIC sizing, inter-node bandwidth?
08:54 Marco Liu: for private GPU clusters we typically recommend 200Gbps per host for multi-GPU topologies; if you use model parallelism or big kv caches across nodes ensure RDMA capable networking. We'll include a sizing note in the on-prem docs.
09:10 Jake Brooks: ok sounds practical. We should aim to have the bench results and docs by next week.
09:16 Alice Kim: noted. Thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts.
09:20 -- End of recording --

References/Artifacts mentioned: benchmarking-playbook (link above), instrumentation patch repo (will attach), example Locust script (will attach), results spreadsheet template (will attach).
